newsitem.title: MEXICO: Banco de Mexico net reserves, assets rise.
newsitem.headline: Banco de Mexico net reserves, assets rise.

text.p: Banco de Mexico said on Tuesday its international reserves as of July 4 were $22.00 billion, compared to $21.695 billion on June 27.
The central bank said that its net international assets as of the same date were $14.568 billion compared to $14.128 billion the week before.
The central bank said the increase of $440 million in net international assets during the period was due to:
--Net income of foreign currency from the federal government worth $58 million.
--The purchase of $218 million from credit institutions, a product of the partial exercising of options on the sale of dollars to the central bank that were issued during the auction of June 30.
--Net income from operations by the state oil company Pemex worth $135 million.

--A net gain of $29 million for a combination of factors including changes in the dollar value of non-dollar assets and liabilities held by the bank; net returns on interest rates and from trading of metals and securities; and net deposits in dollar accounts from commercial banks at the central bank.
The central bank said that as of July 4, the amount of money held in a fund to prepay 2006 notes on August 6 had stayed the same at $4.536 billion.
Banco de Mexico said that between June 27 and July 4 the monetary base rose 822 million pesos, the government's balance at the central bank fell 3.786 billion pesos.
The bank said it undertook monetary regulation operations for a total of 10.701 billion pesos in the same time frame in order to neutralize greater liquidity.
The following tables detail Banco de Mexico's reserves and net domestic credit. All figures are in billions of pesos, unless otherwise indicated.
June 27 July 4
International Reserves
U.S. Dollars $21.695 bln $22.000 bln
Monetary Base 80.532 81.354
Net International Assets*
U.S. Dollars $14.128 bln $14.568 bln
Net Domestic Credit -31.817 -34.695
*Net International Assets are defined as gross international assets minus central bank liabilities with the IMF and assets of less than a six-month duration from other central banks.
((--David Luhnow, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-7902))
